I am seventy-one years old this year, and I have been farming this land in Quzhou since I was a young man. My bones ache a bit more now, but I know this soil like I know my own hands. I never went past primary school, but the land has been my teacher for over fifty years. I do not chase after fancy new ideas — I stick to what works, what has fed my family year after year.

In Quzhou, on the North China Plain, there is really only one sensible way to farm: winter wheat followed by summer maize. This double-cropping system is what the land and the climate allow. If I tried something strange like vegetables or soybeans, I would be taking a big risk, and at my age I cannot afford a bad year. The grain dealers come to the village every harvest; they always buy wheat and maize. It is safe.

I have about 4 mu of good flat land. I will plant all of it. I will use improved seed varieties — not the cheapest traditional seeds, because those do not yield enough anymore, but not the most expensive hybrids either, because the seed cost eats into my thin margin. The improved varieties from the county seed station are a good middle ground. I know them, they germinate well, and I can save some seed if I need to.

For wheat, I will till the land with my small rotary tiller — I do not do deep ploughing anymore, it costs too much diesel and my old tractor struggles. I will spread fertilizer before sowing: urea for nitrogen, and some compound fertilizer for phosphorus and potassium. The wheat needs about three irrigations if the spring is dry — one at green-up, one at jointing, and one at grain-filling. I will spray pesticide twice if the aphids show up, which they usually do. I expect around 450 kg per mu if the weather is normal.

After the wheat harvest in early June, I will immediately plant maize. Timing is everything — every day I delay, I lose yield. I will till again with the rotary tiller and apply fertilizer. Maize needs less fuss than wheat: two irrigations, one when it is knee-high and one at tasseling, and maybe two pesticide sprays. I expect around 550 kg per mu.

I keep my fertilizer rates modest. I have seen young farmers pour on too much nitrogen — it wastes money and the county environmental officers complain. I use just enough to get a good crop without throwing money away.

This is my plan. It is not exciting, but it will put food on the table and maybe leave a little cash for medicine.
